item.title: The Rodman-Cantore connection at Washington Spirit
item.dc:creator: Federico Ninivaggi
item.description:
Nº 15 · football · Nov 21, 2026

The Rodman-Cantore connection at Washington Spirit

In 2026 Rodman has set up ten Washington goals, and Cantore scored five: the most productive pair in the 2026 NWSL.

Football

↩ back to Football

In 2026 Trinity Rodman has set up ten goals for her Washington Spirit teammates, and Sofia Cantore scored five of them, including the equaliser in the semi-final against Utah. In the regular season no NWSL pair scored more. Three others reached four goals, among them a Kansas City Current pair, Washington’s opponents in the final.

Here a pass counts when it is the last pass before the shot, as recorded by American Soccer Analysis, a site that publishes advanced NWSL data. Expected goals, or xG, measure the quality of a shot: the probability that it becomes a goal, from an ASA model.

Rodman’s pass

In the regular season Rodman set up more shots for her teammates than any other Washington player, 35, and more for Cantore than for anyone else. A third of Cantore’s 34 shots that followed a pass came from Rodman, while among her other teammates’ shots Rodman’s share is 14%.

Better chances

In the regular season, Cantore’s shots after a Rodman pass were worth 0.23 xG each, more than twice the 0.10 xG of her other shots. The sample is small, though: eleven shots.

Part of the difference comes from the kind of attack: four of those eleven shots came on the fast break, against two of Cantore’s other 38. Three followed a through ball, while none of the 23 passes from other teammates did.

The limit of the data

Four regular-season goals are few: they came in 3 games, two of them in the first six minutes at Orlando on 2 May, and with one goal fewer the pair would drop among the 10 with three. From Rodman’s passes Cantore scored 4 goals against 2.5 expected, so part of the lead comes from shots that went in more often than their quality suggested.

In the semi-final

Against Utah, Washington fell behind in the second minute to Cloé Lacasse’s goal. In the eighth Rodman set up Cantore’s equaliser, and Clara Luvanga scored the winner in the second half.

How to read it. A pair is the player who makes the last pass before a shot and the player who shoots. Expected goals, or xG, are the probability that a shot becomes a goal: ten shots worth 0.1 xG each add up to one goal on average. The bars and the map cover the 2026 regular season, 30 games per team. Rodman’s ten goals set up cover all 2026 games up to 15 November, playoffs included.

Source: American Soccer Analysis, NWSL 2026.

Federico Ninivaggi · November 21, 2026

item.title: Bethune and Santos: two ways to play the No. 10
item.dc:creator: Federico Ninivaggi
item.description:
Nº 26 · football · Nov 21, 2026

Bethune and Santos: two ways to play the No. 10

In 2026 no NWSL attacking midfielder set up a bigger share of shots on the fast break than Santos and Bethune. With the ball, Santos keeps it moving and Bethune carries it and plays forward.

Football

↩ back to Football

Tonight’s NWSL final brings together the two teams with the league’s highest share of chances on the fast break: Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current. Two of their attacking midfielders, Leicy Santos and Croix Bethune, were the ones who most often set up the final shot of that counter-attack in 2026. With the ball, though, they play in two different ways.

The shared counter-attack

Across the NWSL, 8% of the shots a teammate sets up come on the fast break. For Santos the share rose to 29%, the highest among the 15 attacking midfielders with at least 900 minutes. Bethune was second at 26%. By number of shots, Bethune with 11 and Santos with 10 are first and second in the whole league, in any role.

The two teams rank first and second in the league for the share of shots set up on the fast break, 14% at Washington and 12% at Kansas City. Part of that lead, though, comes from these two players: their teammates reach only 12% and 10%.

The trait belongs to spring and summer: since 1 September Bethune has set up 1 shot of 10 on the fast break, Santos none of 4.

Two ways of using the ball

The two carry equal weight in their teams: in the games she plays Bethune takes 8.7% of Kansas City’s touches and Santos 8.5% of Washington’s, second and third among the 15 attacking midfielders.

Santos keeps the ball moving: no NWSL attacking midfielder passes more often, 45 times per 90 minutes. Her completed passes move the ball 2.0 metres forward on average. They are not short, 16.8 metres on average: the ball travels a long way and gains little ground. Santos keeps possession and circulates it.

Bethune carries the ball and plays forward: among the 15 she ranks first for dribbling actions, 20 per 90 minutes, and second for forward distance per completed pass, 4.7 metres. She passes 33 times per 90 minutes.

Part of the difference comes from the teams: Washington make 56% of the passes in their games, Kansas City 47%. Kansas City also play more directly than Washington: their completed passes move the ball 6.7 metres forward on average, Washington’s 5.2 metres. The gap between the two players, though, is wider than the gap between their teams.

Where the chances come from

Corners shape Santos’s chances: 11 of the 35 shots she set up came from one, all inside the box. Bethune set up 6 of her 43 shots from set pieces: the other 37 came from open play, settled or on the break.

How to read it. The data come from American Soccer Analysis, a site that publishes advanced NWSL statistics. The comparison is with the league’s 15 attacking midfielders, by the site’s position, with at least 900 minutes in 2026: Bethune played 2,505, Santos 2,039. The minutes include stoppage time, so per-90 figures are 10% to 12% lower than per-game ones. A shot set up is one that follows the player’s last pass. The touch share counts only the games the player appeared in. Dribbling actions are those the site groups under dribbling: carries, take-ons, miscontrols and dispossessions. The figures cover all 2026 games up to 15 November: the regular season, the playoffs and one June knockout game.

Source: American Soccer Analysis, NWSL 2026.

Federico Ninivaggi · November 21, 2026

item.title: AC Boise’s points matched its chances, among League One’s best
item.dc:creator: Federico Ninivaggi
item.description:
Nº 20 · football · Nov 18, 2026

AC Boise’s points matched its chances, among League One’s best

Athletic Club Boise’s first League One season, read through public shot data: chances among the league’s best, points to match, a stronger second half, and a final lost late at Charlotte.

Football

↩ back to Football

Over the regular season, Athletic Club Boise created and allowed chances worth as many points as those of any team in USL League One. It finished with close to the points those chances deserved.

In the second half of the season Boise created more than in the first without allowing more, and its points rose further still because it conceded fewer goals from chances of similar value.

The title went to Charlotte Independence, which won far more points than its own chances deserved, the widest gap in the league.

In the final Boise led until the closing minutes, yet across both games played at Charlotte’s home stadiums the hosts created more, even while the game was tied.

Athletic Club Boise ended its first season in USL League One, the third tier of American professional soccer, with a lost final and a place among the league’s best teams by the quality of its chances. Over the regular season its points came out close to where those chances put them, and the final went 4-2 to Charlotte Independence, a team that beat its own chances by a wider margin than anyone else.

It matters because Boise moves up to the USL Championship, the second tier, next season at the league’s invitation, as KIVI reported. A team that lost points to bad luck could expect them back without changing anything, and Boise’s numbers offer no such comfort, although they also describe a side that improved as the year went on. According to Idaho News, the club was only the second expansion team to reach the final in its first season.

How the chances are counted

The data come from American Soccer Analysis, or ASA, the site that publishes advanced data for North American leagues, League One shots included. Each shot carries a value in expected goals, or xG: the probability that a shot of that kind, from that spot, becomes a goal. A team’s xG adds up to the goals its chances were worth, and ASA turns the xG of a game into expected points, the points those chances would bring.1

1 ASA’s glossary defines expected points as “Expected team points earned based on xG (team model)”.

This league needs its own yardstick. League One teams scored about nine goals for each ten expected over the regular season, so falling short of xG is normal here. In what follows, a team’s goals are measured against that league rate rather than against the model.

Among the best three by chances

By ASA’s measure, Boise’s chances were worth 1.78 expected points a game, the highest figure in the division by a hair over Union Omaha and Forward Madison. Defence was the base of it, since no other team allowed chances of lower value.

In the chart each dot is a team, placed by expected points per game across and by points per game up. A team on the dashed line won what its chances deserved, and a team above it won more. Boise is on the line, with 58 points against an expected tally of 56.8.

That near match came by a narrower road than the total suggests. Measured against the league rate, Boise scored about four goals fewer than its chances implied and conceded about three more than the shots against it were worth. The two strikers with the most valuable chances account for more than the whole shortfall up front: between them they scored 14 goals from chances that would have produced about 19 at the league rate.

Close games brought the points back. Of the 25 league games that Boise drew or decided by a single goal it lost only five, and just one team had a better record in such games.

A stronger second half

Boise’s chances grew in value through the year, from 1.57 expected goals a game in the first half of the league season to 2.03 in the second, while the value of what it allowed barely changed.

The chart follows the average of the previous eight league games, in which the green line tracks the xG Boise created and the grey line the xG it allowed, and after the dashed midseason line the green climbs while the grey stays flat. The rise showed away from home as well, although over seven and nine away games a difference of that size is within what chance produces.

Points rose more than the chances alone would explain. Over the second half expected points grew by about four and actual points by ten, largely because Boise conceded 16 goals from shots after 22 in the first half, from chances allowed of similar value. Part of the second-half level therefore rests on goals conceded below the value of the chances allowed, a gap that may not last.

Charlotte, 17 points above its chances

Charlotte Independence finished first from chances whose value ranked only sixth, and in ASA’s data no other team came within ten points of its surplus.

That surplus came from both ends of the pitch. By the league rate, Charlotte scored about nine goals more than its chances implied and conceded about twelve fewer than the shots against it were worth, which gave it the best goal difference in the division.

Gaps of this kind run both ways. Greenville Triumph SC and New York Cosmos each fell between thirteen and fifteen points short of their chances, while for the rest of the league the spread between points and expected points is about six points over a season. Shot data cannot say how much of Charlotte’s surplus came from its goalkeeper, from its finishers or from its opponents’ misses.

Corners and the road

Corners gave Boise 15% of its expected goals, against 12% for the league as a whole, and no team allowed less from them. Both totals are small, worth fewer than ten goals over the season, so a handful of headers either way would change the ranking.

On average, a team’s xG difference in League One was about 0.9 goals a game better at home than away. Boise was the only team whose chances on the road outweighed those it allowed, by a margin that chance alone could produce.

The three games at the end

Boise opened the playoffs as it had played the season, with a 2-0 home win over One Knoxville in which it allowed almost no chances. Against Chattanooga Red Wolves it needed extra time and a single goal to go through, after taking more than twice as many shots as its opponent.

The final was played at the Sportsplex at Matthews, one of the two stadiums where Charlotte played its home games. Charlotte had won the regular season, and with it home field throughout the playoffs. Boise led at the break, according to Idaho News, and was still ahead 2-1 in the closing minutes, before Charlotte scored three late goals.

Chances explain the defeat better than luck does, although less sharply than the totals suggest. Over the whole final Charlotte’s chances were worth far more than Boise’s, but 57% of Charlotte’s expected goals came while it was chasing the game, when any side pushes forward. While the game was tied, Charlotte still created chances worth 1.3 expected goals to Boise’s 0.8.

The May meeting at the American Legion Memorial Stadium, where Charlotte played most of its home games, had gone the same way. With the game level Charlotte created by far the better chances, a missed penalty among them, and won by a single goal. In Boise in September the balance reversed and the game ended level.

What the season says

By the chances it created and allowed, Boise’s first season was that of a top side, and its points matched those chances over the year. The second half was stronger in chances and stronger still in results, helped by fewer goals conceded. Charlotte, the champion, ran further ahead of its numbers than anyone, and at home it outplayed Boise twice.

For Boise’s staff and supporters, the reading changes what to expect from last season’s evidence.

  • Expect no rebound from luck over a full season, because Boise’s points already matched its chances in League One.
  • Judge the first months on the chances created and allowed, since in this league the table drifted from them by three points or more for most teams.

The reading rests on one season in the third tier. Next season brings stronger opponents and a changed squad, and nothing in League One data measures how Boise’s chances will travel up a level. ASA owns the xG model, and no source this piece could check publishes how well it fits League One. A fit on this league alone would show whether the missing goals belong to the model or to the players. This piece uses shot data only, leaving aside ASA’s values for passing and ball-winning, and public data for this league do not record injuries.

How this piece was made. Data from the public interface of American Soccer Analysis for the 2026 USL League One season, retrieved on 18 November. ASA records every regular-season game but two, both of them Chattanooga home games. Expected goals are the sum of ASA’s xG for each shot; expected points are ASA’s own figure, built on its team-level xG model, which differs slightly from the shot-by-shot sum. The season is split after the first half of the league games, and a split at the start of July gives the same picture. Goals compared with xG exclude own goals, which have no shot attached, and ASA may still revise the shots of the final in the days after it.

Federico Ninivaggi · November 18, 2026

item.title: Best on the break meets hardest to break in the NWSL final
item.dc:creator: Federico Ninivaggi
item.description:
Nº 17 · football · Nov 17, 2026

Best on the break meets hardest to break in the NWSL final

Saturday brings together the team that creates most on the fast break and the one that allows the fewest fast-break shots.

Football

↩ back to Football

On Saturday 21 November, at Audi Field in Washington, the NWSL final brings together two teams that finished the regular season almost level: Washington Spirit third and Kansas City Current fourth, two points behind. Kansas City create more on the fast break than any other team in the league, and Washington allow the fewest fast-break shots.

Kansas City’s weapon

Kansas City scored 14 fast-break goals in the regular season, four times the league median. Their fast-break chances were also the best in the NWSL, measured in expected goals, or xG: the probability that a shot becomes a goal, from the model of American Soccer Analysis, the site that publishes advanced NWSL data.

A strong attack does not explain the lead on its own, because nearly a fifth of Kansas City’s xG comes from fast breaks, a larger share than any other team draws from them. Much of the weapon belongs to Temwa Chawinga. The forward scored six fast-break goals, more than any other player in the league, and on her own she produces two-fifths of her team’s fast-break xG.

Kansas City need a lead to defend, though: more than half of their fast-break goals came with the score already in their favour, when opponents were chasing and likely left more space behind. Across the league, a little over a third of fast-break shots come with a lead. At Kansas City, half do.

Washington’s defence

Washington allowed 14 fast-break shots in 30 games, fewer than any other team, but they paid for the few they gave up: five went in.

Washington break often too: no team took more fast-break shots, although their chances are worth less than Kansas City’s. Trinity Rodman took half of those shots, from worse positions than Chawinga, and on average her chances are worth less than half of the Kansas City forward’s. She scored once on the fast break in the regular season, while in other phases of play she scored more than her chances promised, 11 goals from 8 expected.

In the quarter-final against Portland on 8 November, Rodman scored twice on the fast break in Washington’s 4-1 win.

The two meetings

In the two regular-season games between the finalists the fast break almost disappeared. In April Washington won 4-0 at home, with only three fast-break shots between the two teams.

In October Kansas City won 2-1 at home without a single fast-break shot, even though they created less than Washington. In the playoffs all of their goals came from dead balls, the penalty included, and in two games they took one fast-break shot.

What to watch on Saturday

A single game has few fast breaks: Kansas City have taken a little over one per game this season, and Washington have allowed fewer than one in two games. So the first goal may matter more than usual. Should Kansas City score first, Washington would have to push forward and open the space that players like Chawinga look for. Should Washington score first, Kansas City would have to build against one of the teams that keep the ball most in the NWSL.

How to read it. A fast break is a shot that American Soccer Analysis tags as “Fastbreak”. The site does not publish the definition, and here it is read as a quick attack after the ball is won back. Ten shots worth 0.1 xG each add up to one goal on average. The figures cover the regular season, 30 games per team, and playoff figures are given separately.

Source: American Soccer Analysis, NWSL 2026, regular season and playoffs to 15 November 2026.

Federico Ninivaggi · November 17, 2026

item.title: When a public guarantee is voided, the working paper in a video
item.dc:creator: Federico Ninivaggi
item.description:
Nº 18 · video · Nov 17, 2026

When a public guarantee is voided, the working paper in a video

Italy’s Central Guarantee Fund refuses to pay if the bank screened the loan without due diligence: the argument of the working paper and the case of Banca Progetto.

Markets and creditPublic policy

↩ back to Video

Italy’s Central Guarantee Fund repays the bank most of a small-firm loan that goes unpaid. The repayment is voided if the bank screened the loan without due diligence, and the working paper «Guarantees That Negligence Voids» studies what this does to the bank’s incentives and to its capital. The video follows the argument to the case of Banca Progetto in under two minutes.

The figures in the video come from the manuscript. The full abstract is on the Research page.

Nº 12 · football · Nov 16, 2026

Frida Maanum’s match against London City

Her touches, passes, ball wins and shots in the 1-1 draw of 15 November 2026, on one graphic.

Football

↩ back to Football

First WSL start of the season for Frida Maanum, and all three of Arsenal’s big chances went through her: she scored the opener, set up a second and had the third saved at 1-1 in the 77th minute. In all she had a hand in 9 of Arsenal’s 17 shots.

How to read it. A big chance is a clear scoring chance. A key pass is the pass before a teammate’s shot. A progressive pass is completed, gains at least a tenth of the pitch and cuts the distance to the goal line by at least a quarter. The heat map blurs each of her 49 touches over about 14 metres. Ball wins are balls won back by recoveries, interceptions or tackles, counted once per ball.

item.title: Planned AI power is heading to smaller US cities
item.dc:creator: Federico Ninivaggi
item.description:
Nº 10 · charts · Nov 14, 2026

Planned AI power is heading to smaller US cities

Where the large AI data centers tracked by Epoch AI plan their power, county by county.

Artificial intelligencePlaces

↩ back to Charts

Smaller American cities hold under a third of the population and more than half of the power planned for large AI data centers.

The map shows the 77 large AI data centers in the United States tracked by the research institute Epoch AI. The solid disc is the power each site draws today and the ring the power planned by 2030. Blue counties belong to metro areas under one million people, grey counties to metro areas of one million or more, and pale counties are nonmetro.

The bars below compare the three types of county. Nonmetro counties cover two thirds of the land, yet their share of planned power stays close to their share of Americans. Ordinary data centers mapped by volunteers on OpenStreetMap are mostly in big cities. The smaller cities hold about two fifths of the AI power drawn today and more than half of the power planned.

The two largest planned sites, Microsoft Fairwater in Racine County, Wisconsin, and OpenAI Stargate in Doña Ana County, New Mexico, are in smaller cities. The largest rural project, OpenAI Stargate Shackelford in Texas, is planned in a county of about three thousand residents.

For utilities and regional planners in metro areas under one million people, the chart shows that most planned AI power is headed to places like theirs.

Sources: Epoch AI, Frontier Data Centers, data of November 5, 2026, CC-BY 4.0 license; USDA Economic Research Service, Rural-Urban Continuum Codes 2023; US Census Bureau, county boundaries 2023; © OpenStreetMap contributors, downloaded on October 5, 2026, ODbL license.

item.title: The markets’ new heavyweight borrower
item.dc:creator: Federico Ninivaggi
item.description:
Nº 04 · long read · Oct 6, 2026

The markets’ new heavyweight borrower

In twenty-one months Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle placed 325.7 billion dollars of bonds, with maturities worthy of government debt.

Artificial intelligenceMarkets and credit

↩ back to Long read

Between March and June 2026 Microsoft added 133 billion dollars to an item that does not appear on its balance sheet. The item collects the rents, mostly for data centers, that the group has committed to pay under contracts already signed but not yet commenced: 196.6 billion dollars at the end of March, 329.1 billion dollars at the end of June. Over the same period Microsoft did not register a single bond issue with the US securities regulator, as it has not since January 2025. Microsoft’s case is the extreme one of a trend that has been reshaping the credit market for almost two years. The groups building the infrastructure of artificial intelligence commit to paying huge sums in two forms: bonds, which are debt and appear on the balance sheet, and leases already signed, which the balance sheet does not show and which appear only in the notes.1

1 Microsoft, 10-Q as of March 31, 2026 and 10-K as of June 30, 2026, note on leases: “additional leases, primarily for datacenters, that had not yet commenced”. No final bond prospectus, 424B2 or 424B5, filed by Microsoft since January 1, 2025.

In the industry these groups are called hyperscalers: they run computing centers on a planetary scale and sell their capacity, and they are Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and, in the classification of the Financial Times, Oracle. Their debt is measured on the documents that companies must file with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the SEC, which supervises US markets, and on the portfolios that mutual funds disclose every quarter.

A new borrower

From January 2025 to September 2026 the four groups that finance themselves on the bond market filed 21 final bond prospectuses, for 136 securities and 325.7 billion dollars. Alphabet placed 110.5 billion dollars, Amazon 109.5 billion, Meta 55.0 billion and Oracle 50.8 billion. In the first nine months of 2026 the total placed reached 217.4 billion dollars, 2.0 times that of the whole of 2025.2

2 SEC, 424B2 and 424B5 final prospectuses and term sheets, 82 documents downloaded on September 29, 2026; amounts in dollars at the exchange rate of the issue date. In all 21 offerings the amount underwritten by the banks matches the stated total. The register is a lower bound: it excludes issues placed outside the SEC perimeter and the data center vehicles.

The debt is no longer denominated in dollars alone. Almost a quarter of the amount issued, 23.2 percent, is denominated in other currencies: 42.4 billion dollars in euros, 16.3 billion in Canadian dollars, 13.2 billion in sterling and 3.6 billion in yen. In May 2026 Alphabet placed 576.5 billion yen in seven securities, the last maturing in 2066. The choice of five currencies suggests an issuer looking for buyers in every market.3

3 Register of tranches from SEC prospectuses; values in dollars at the exchange rate of the day. Total denominated in dollars: 250.2 billion dollars.

4 January-August 2026: 157 billion dollars issued in dollars by the hyperscalers, 212 billion in all currencies, equal to 10 percent of the increase in marketable Treasury debt, Monthly Statement of the Public Debt. F. Ninivaggi, “Il conto della guerra arriva sui titoli di Stato”, LinkedIn, October 2026, in Italian.

The amounts remain small next to government bonds. Between January and August 2026 the hyperscalers’ dollar issues weighed about a tenth of the debt added by the US Treasury, and their calendar does not follow that of government bond yields: the rise in Treasury yields in 2026 has mostly different causes, as an earlier analysis showed. The novelty is in the corporate credit market.4

Debt for a generation

The average maturity of the 136 securities, weighted by amount, is 16.6 years. 29.3 percent of the amount issued matures in thirty years or more, 10.6 percent in forty years or more. Alphabet and Amazon placed fifty-year securities, and in February 2026 Alphabet issued in sterling a security that matures in 2126. On the fixed-coupon securities alone the four groups pay about 15.9 billion dollars of interest every year.5

5 Maturity at the issue date, weighted by amount. Alphabet sterling bond with a 6.125 percent coupon maturing in 2126, 424B2 prospectus filed on February 12, 2026.

The cost of those maturities has grown. On its forty-year bond Meta paid a coupon of 5.75 percent in October 2025 and 6.45 percent in April 2026, and Alphabet went from 5.30 percent in April 2025 to 6.50 percent in August 2026. Meta’s balance sheet at June 30, 2026 shows the weight of long maturities: on bonds outstanding of 84.00 billion dollars, the interest still to be paid until maturity amounts to 89.38 billion dollars, more than the principal itself.6

6 Coupons from the prospectuses; pricing dates October 30, 2025 and April 30, 2026. Meta, 10-Q as of June 30, 2026: “$84.00 billion aggregate principal amount of Notes outstanding”, future interest of 4.40 billion dollars within twelve months and 84.98 billion beyond.

The price of risk

The cost of a corporate bond is measured by its spread, that is the extra yield over the US Treasury of the same maturity, expressed in basis points: 85 basis points correspond to 0.85 percent a year. Rating classes should order spreads, so that an AA issuer pays less than an A issuer. In April 2025 Alphabet, rated AA+, placed its ten-year bond at 47 basis points over the Treasury. In August 2026 it paid 85 basis points, 38 basis points more. On the same two dates the average spread of AA bonds stood still at 57 basis points, and that of A bonds fell from 86 to 65 basis points. While the market asked less of A-class borrowers, it asked more of a borrower rated AA+: in August 2026 Alphabet placed above the average of the class below.7

7 Spreads stated in Alphabet’s term sheets, FWP, with trade dates of April 28, 2025 and August 6, 2026, “Spread to Benchmark Treasury”, the second filed on August 7, with the ratings stated in the same sheets. ICE BofA indexes of US AA and A bonds, from FRED, same day; the values of August 6 and 7, 2026 coincide. On the forty-year bond Alphabet’s spread rose by 60 basis points. A index: 86 basis points on April 28, 2025, 65 basis points on August 6, 2026. The spread at placement contains the premium needed to place a large offering in a single day, which the index of bonds already outstanding does not have: the overtaking of the A-class average should be read with this caution, while changes over time are comparable.

8 Event study on 12 dollar issues; average change on the other days of the same period -0.2 basis points; the widening exceeds 99.9 percent of the averages obtained by randomly drawing twelve days without issues, 10,000 draws. Excluding the windows that straddle the month-end index rebalancing: +2.9 basis points, 99.4th percentile. AAA index: +2.8 basis points, with an increase in 92 percent of the events. The AA index includes, according to FRED, “all securities with a given investment grade rating AA”; the presence of Alphabet bonds is inferred from the AA+ rating in the term sheets, note 7, not verified on the composition of the index.

The large issues also seem to move the rest of the market. Between the day before the pricing of the 12 most significant dollar issues and the third day after, the average spread of AA bonds widens on average by 2.6 basis points, against an almost zero change on the other days of the same period. The AA index, however, collects bonds rated AA, and Alphabet is rated AA+, so its widening may include the repricing of Alphabet bonds already outstanding. The index of the class above, AAA, which includes no bonds rated AA, widens by 2.8 basis points around the same events. The widening of the AA index recurs in 83 percent of the events and affects all rating classes alike. With twelve events, many of which fall a few days after quarterly results, the effect of supply cannot be fully separated from that of news on investment.8

The commitments off the balance sheet

A company’s leverage is usually measured by the ratio of debt to the cash its business generates. For the hyperscalers this measure captures a minority of their commitments. US accounting standards require leases in progress to be recognized on the balance sheet, while leases signed but not yet commenced remain in the notes, and in this form the hyperscalers secure the data centers that others will build for them.9

9 Financial statements distinguish the recognized “lease liabilities” from the “leases that have not yet commenced”, reported in the notes.

10 SEC, XBRL data from financial statements and text of the notes to 10-K and 10-Q filings as of June 30, 2026, with some exceptions: for Oracle, debt and leases not yet commenced as of May 31, 2026, recognized leases as of August 31, 2026; for Meta, finance leases as of December 31, 2025; for CoreWeave, shown only in the figure, debt as of March 31, 2026. Leases not yet commenced: Microsoft 329.1 billion dollars, Meta 279.0 billion, Oracle 260.0 billion, Amazon 137.2 billion, Alphabet 85.2 billion. Microsoft: “with some arrangements subject to certain contractual conditions being met”. Purchase commitments are left out of the count, as they include items other than leases, such as energy contracts and licenses.

In mid-2026 the five groups report 485.9 billion dollars of financial debt and 292.6 billion dollars of leases on the balance sheet. Leases signed and not yet commenced amount to 1,090.5 billion dollars, 2.2 times financial debt. They are not debt in the strict sense: they are future payments, not discounted, under contracts that last up to thirty years, and some of Microsoft’s contracts depend on conditions still to be met. They do, however, give the order of magnitude of fixed commitments that in some cases grow faster than debt. Between March and June 2026 Microsoft’s item grew by more than Meta raised with all the bonds it has issued since 2025, and Meta’s item grew in six months, from December 2025 to June 2026, from 103.77 to 278.99 billion dollars.10

Meta also uses a third form. In October 2025 it set up with a fund of the Blue Owl group a joint company to build a data center campus in Louisiana. It owns 20 percent of the company and does not consolidate it. The partner financed its share by privately placing 27.3 billion dollars of secured bonds, which do not appear on Meta’s balance sheet. Meta’s maximum exposure to loss, given in the notes to its accounts, is 46.03 billion dollars, 55 percent of the financial debt it recognizes.11

Blue Owl Real Estate Net Lease Trust, 10-Q as of September 30, 2025, note 18: “Beignet Investor issued $27,293,849 in senior secured notes with an interest rate of 6.581% and a maturity date of May 30, 2049”, amounts in thousands of dollars. In the N-PORT 2026q2 archives the security appears as “BEIGNET INVESTOR LLC 144A 6.581000% 05/30/2049”, CUSIP 076912AA2: Rule 144A restricts the placement to institutional investors, outside registered prospectuses.

Free cash flow computed as operating cash flow minus gross investment in plant: Amazon -11.6 billion dollars, Oracle -28.7 billion. Amazon instead subtracts investment net of sales and incentives and reports a different figure: “Free cash flow decreased to an outflow of $7.6 billion for the trailing twelve months”, 8-K of July 30, 2026, exhibit 99.1. Oracle, 10-K as of May 31, 2026: “Remaining performance obligations were $638 billion and $138 billion as of May 31, 2026 and 2025, respectively”. “Years of cash” are a measure of scale, not a repayment plan.

Against these commitments, the operating cash flow of the five groups was 707.3 billion dollars over the last twelve months, and investment in plant absorbs 82.9 percent of that cash. Amazon invested 107 percent of its operating cash flow and Oracle 161 percent, and both closed the last twelve months with negative free cash flow. Oracle’s profile is the most stretched: debt and leases, recognized or still to commence, are worth 9.2 years of its operating cash flow, even though the group reports 638 billion dollars of customer contracts already signed and not yet performed.12

Who buys the debt

US mutual funds and ETFs file with the SEC the full list of their holdings every quarter. In the portfolios of February-April 2026 the debt of the artificial intelligence ecosystem, that is the debt of the hyperscalers and of the companies that build or run computing capacity for them, was worth 80.2 billion dollars, against 30.8 billion dollars a year earlier: 2.6 times as much. Oracle is the most widely held borrower, present in 1,190 funds that hold 21.0 percent of its financial debt.13

13 SEC, Form N-PORT archives 2025q2 and 2026q2, latest report per fund, portfolios mostly of February-March. Ecosystem: hyperscalers, Meta’s vehicle, CoreWeave and other computing companies, data center securitizations, SoftBank, Nvidia. Oracle debt as of May 31, 2026. N-PORT describes only registered US funds: insurers, pension funds, banks and foreign investors are left out.

14 N-PORT 2026q2, aggregation by fund family. The index fund mechanism is an inference about how such funds work, not a measured fact.

Four fund families, Vanguard, BlackRock, Capital Group and PIMCO, hold 60.1 percent of the ecosystem’s debt held by US funds. The first two manage mostly index funds, which do not select securities but buy them in proportion to the amount outstanding. The more the hyperscalers issue, the more their debt enters the portfolios of those who have chosen to replicate the whole bond market, and issuers would thus find a buyer that, by construction, does not negotiate on price.14

Concentration has also grown. In the 2025 portfolios a single US fund with more than 100 million dollars in assets had over 5 percent of its assets in this debt, and in the 2026 portfolios the funds above that threshold number 37. Funds above 2 percent of assets went from 65 to 269. US funds hold 36 percent of the value of the bonds of Meta’s vehicle, and only 19.0 percent of that value is held by funds that also own Meta bonds. Those who hold both have an exposure to the group larger than the one they read under the heading “Meta”.15

15 Funds with more than 100 million dollars in assets. Beignet Investor bonds in funds: 9.7 billion dollars in 317 funds, of which 6.9 billion at PIMCO.

The labs downstream

The leases signed by the hyperscalers are paid back by the computing contracts that others sign with them, and among the largest of these customers are two unlisted companies, Anthropic and OpenAI, which do not file financial statements with the SEC. The effects appear in the accounts of those who finance them. In the second quarter of 2026 Amazon recorded 53.4 billion dollars of non-operating income, “primarily from our investments in Anthropic”, about two thirds of its pre-tax income for the quarter. The revaluation of Anthropic’s preferred shares alone, 50.5 billion dollars, is worth 1.8 times the quarter’s operating income. The ability of these labs to raise the money with which they pay for computing capacity, and therefore the leases on which data center construction rests, depends largely on their valuation.16

Operating income for the quarter 27.5 billion dollars, pre-tax income 80.9 billion.

The comparison with the railways

A recurring comparison is with the building of the railways in the nineteenth century. In 1847, at the peak of the British Railway Mania, railway investment absorbed 7.3 percent of British gross domestic product, while the 745 billion dollars of investment announced for 2026 by Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft is worth 2.4 percent of 2025 US gross domestic product. For credit, the difference that matters concerns financing. The acts of Parliament that authorized the British companies usually allowed borrowing of up to a third of share capital, and when the bubble burst the losses fell on shareholders, while almost no line went bankrupt. The American railways were built mainly with debt, in a corporate bond market then made up mostly of railroad, canal and mining securities: over 1873-1875 the annual default rates of that market added up to 35.9 percent of its par value.17

The two models now coexist. On financial debt alone, modest relative to the operating cash flow they generate, the large groups other than Oracle resemble the British companies. Counting the leases already signed, the resemblance fades. The American model resurfaces at the margins, in the vehicles that build data centers with debt and in the computing companies, tied to the large groups by long-term leases. Anyone who wished to measure these commitments could look, beyond bond issuance, at the line in the notes to the accounts that collects leases not yet commenced, where commitments grew faster than debt between December 2025 and June 2026 for Meta, and in the second quarter of 2026 alone for Microsoft.
